## Lesson Overview
- **Topic:** Unit 3: Mystery and Magic
- **Grade:** Grade 8
- **Subject:** English
- **Duration:** 40-45 minutes
- **CBSE Unit:** Unit 3: Mystery and Magic ("The Case of the Fifth Word" - Encyclopedia Brown, and reported-question grammar drawn from the story)

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:
1. Explain how Encyclopedia Brown uses context - the calendar sheet, the crime, and the nursery - to decode the four strange words as altered weekday names.
2. Apply the story's code pattern (dropping d-a-y and rearranging the remaining letters) to work out the unwritten fifth word and its meaning in the mystery.
3. Convert a direct question from the story into a reported question, using correct declarative word order.

## Prerequisites
Students should already know:
- The plot of "The Case of the Fifth Word" from an earlier reading lesson in this unit.
- The basic idea of a direct question (a question in quotation marks) from earlier grammar lessons.

## Materials & Resources
- NCERT Textbook Grade 8 English
- Blackboard / Whiteboard
- One puzzle handout per pair showing the four words "Nom Utes Sweden Hurts" and space to work out the fifth word (teacher-prepared, based only on the chapter content)

## Lesson Plan (Step-by-Step)

### Introduction & Hook (5 minutes)
- Write "Nom Utes Sweden Hurts" on the board and ask: "These four words look meaningless. If I told you they were clipped to a calendar page, would that change how you read them?"
- Take 2-3 guesses, then tell students today's lesson is about solving this exact mystery the way Encyclopedia Brown does - by using context, not just the dictionary.

### Direct Instruction (13 minutes)
- **Chunk 1 - the mystery set-up:** Recap that Nolan clips a calendar sheet with Davenport's address and the four strange words to his will before he dies. Ask: "Why does Mrs Brown's dictionary explanation of each word separately fail to solve the case?" (Expect: she looks at each word alone, ignoring that it's written on a calendar page connected to a hidden-jewellery case.) Clarify that Encyclopedia succeeds because he links the words to their physical context - a calendar - and their purpose - pointing to a hiding place.
- **Chunk 2 - cracking the code:** Show on the board: Monday minus d-a-y leaves "Mon", rearranged as "Nom"; Tuesday minus d-a-y leaves "Tues", rearranged as "Utes". Ask: "Using the same rule, what do Wednesday and Thursday become?" (Expect: Wednesday minus d-a-y rearranges to Sweden; Thursday minus d-a-y rearranges to Hurts.) Confirm as a class.
- **Chunk 3 - the unwritten fifth word:** Ask: "The note only gives four words. Which weekday comes next, and what do you get when you remove d-a-y from it?" (Expect: Friday, which becomes "Fir".) Clarify that this works because Nolan grew a young fir tree in his palm-tree nursery - so the code names an actual hiding place, not just a word game.
- **Chunk 4 - reported speech in the story:** Read aloud the direct question "Is there a young fir tree in Mr Nolan's palm-tree nursery?" Ask: "How would Mrs Brown report this question to Chief Brown?" Model the shift: reporting verb (asked/inquired) + whether/if + declarative word order ("...whether there was a young fir tree..."). Point out that the question mark and quotation marks disappear.

### Guided Practice (10 minutes)
- On the board, guide the class through rearranging "Sweden" and "Hurts" back into Wednesday and Thursday together, confirming the letter-dropping rule as a group before students try it alone.
- Give students two more direct questions from the story context (for example, "Did Nolan hide the jewellery in the nursery?" and "What do the four words mean?") and have pairs orally convert them to reported questions, with teacher circulating to check word order and the if/whether rule.
- Correct any pair that keeps question word order after "whether" or forgets to shift the reporting verb.

### Student Activity (12 minutes)
- In pairs, students complete ONE puzzle handout: (1) work out the fifth word by removing d-a-y from Friday and explain what it reveals about the hiding place; (2) in 2-3 sentences, explain why Encyclopedia's context-based reasoning succeeds where Mrs Brown's word-by-word explanation fails; (3) convert one given direct question from the story into a correctly reported question.
- Teacher circulates, listening for the two misconceptions below and prompting pairs to reread the relevant part of the story if their reasoning strays from the text.
- Two or three pairs share their fifth-word answer and their reported question with the class in the final minutes of this stage.

### Assessment & Closure (5 minutes)
- Quick formative checks aligned to the core objectives:
  - Why couldn't the four words be solved just by looking each one up in a dictionary? (Objective 1)
  - What is the fifth word, and how does it point to the jewellery's hiding place? (Objective 2)
  - Report this question: "Is there a young fir tree in the nursery?" (Objective 3)
- Brief class summary: one student explains, in their own words, why context matters as much as language skill in solving this kind of mystery.
- Exit ticket: In 2-3 sentences, explain how Encyclopedia Brown worked out the fifth word and why it matters to the case.

## Homework Assignment
- Choose any two direct questions Chief Brown or Mrs Brown might reasonably have asked during the case, and rewrite each as a reported question, following the pattern practised in class (reporting verb + if/whether + declarative order).

## Differentiation Strategies
- **For students needing additional support:** Provide the completed Monday-to-Nom and Tuesday-to-Utes examples as models before asking students to work out Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday; give a sentence starter for the reported question ("Mrs Brown asked Chief Brown whether..."); allow pair support throughout the puzzle handout.
- **For students ready for extension:** Ask students to explain why the code would fail if the note had not been clipped to a calendar page (what other context clue does the story rely on?), and to write one additional reported question of their own based on a different moment in the story.

## Common Misconceptions to Address
1. Students may think the four words can be solved as an ordinary vocabulary or dictionary exercise, missing that the calendar context and the crime's purpose are what make the code solvable.
2. Students may keep question word order after "if" or "whether" when reporting a question (for example, "whether was there a fir tree"), instead of using declarative order ("whether there was a fir tree").

## NCERT Alignment
- Grade 8 English, Unit 3: Mystery and Magic - "The Case of the Fifth Word", and the unit's grammar strand on reported Wh- and yes/no questions, as presented in the chapter's own worked example on reporting the fir-tree question.
